title: Double crochet (UK)
subtitle: UK double crochet equals US single crochet — the densest of the basic stitches
excerpt: Double crochet is the smallest worked stitch and the densest. In UK pattern shorthand it's "dc"; US patterns call exactly the same move "single crochet". One of the two famous UK-US confusions in crochet — settle the convention before you start.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), the foundational "plain stitch" in the crochet chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Crochet — the standard British double crochet across the late-Victorian pattern series.

glossaryTerms.definition: The short chain at the start of each new row or round that brings the working yarn up to the height of the next stitch. UK double crochet uses a 1-chain turning chain that does not count as a stitch.

Two parallel naming systems for crochet stitches. UK 'double crochet' is the same move US patterns call 'single crochet'. The whole publication writes UK shorthand by default; the reader-side terminology toggle in the page header flips abbreviations to US.

heroPrompt: A small swatch of double crochet (UK) in cream DK cotton, eight rows worked, sitting flat on a pale linen background — the stitches show as close-packed V-shapes with a dense even texture.

content.text: Double crochet is the smallest worked stitch and the densest. You insert the hook, yarn over, pull a loop through, yarn over, pull through both loops. About 5 mm tall in DK cotton at 4 mm hook tension. The fabric is firm, close-knit, and holds its shape — the right choice for dishcloths, baskets, amigurumi, and any piece that needs structure rather than drape.
A note on terminology. "Double crochet" in UK patterns is the same move that US patterns call "single crochet". UK "dc" equals US "sc". This is one of the two famous

mismatches — the other being treble (UK) versus double crochet (US). Pick a convention before you start a pattern and stick to it. The whole publication writes UK shorthand by default; the reader-side terminology toggle in the page header flips to US if you prefer.

attrs.title: What you need for a learning swatch
attrs.body: 20 g of plain DK-weight cotton in a light colour. A 4 mm hook. A tapestry needle for sewing in tails at the end. Scissors. Good light. Cotton is the right learning yarn because it shows the stitches clearly and doesn't split when the hook enters.

content.text: Start with a slip knot. Chain 11 (ten chains for a 10-stitch row, plus one extra for the turning chain). Count carefully — the live loop on the hook doesn't count.

Row 1: insert the hook into the second chain from the hook (the first chain is the turning chain and stays empty). Yarn over, pull a loop back through the chain. Two loops on the hook. Yarn over again. Pull through both loops. One loop on the hook — the first double crochet is finished.
Work one double crochet in each of the next 9 chains. You now have 10 double crochet stitches in the row.
Row 2 and on: turn the work. Ch 1 (this is the
— does not count as a stitch). Work 1 dc in the first stitch (the very same stitch the hook is in, NOT skipped). Work 1 dc in each of the next 9 stitches. (10 sts.)
Repeat row 2 for as many rows as you want. Eight rows is enough to see the texture clearly. Fasten off, sew in the tails.
What a good double crochet looks like

A neat double crochet shows a clean V-shape at the top, no visible post, and sits flush against the row below. The fabric should be firm but not stiff. In DK cotton at 4 mm hook tension, expect about 18 stitches across 10 cm and about 22 rows across 10 cm. If your stitches look loopy and uneven, your tension is too loose — try a 3.5 mm hook. If they look squashed and the fabric feels like cardboard, tension is too tight — try a 4.5 mm.

attrs.heading: When the swatch doesn't look right
attrs.intro: Four problems beginners hit on the first double crochet swatch.

items.symptom: The swatch grows narrower row by row
items.cause: You skipped the first stitch of each new row (treating the turning chain as the first stitch). With a 1-chain turning chain that does not count, the first stitch is the one directly below.
items.fix: After turning and chaining 1, work the first dc into the very first stitch. Count to 10 at the end of every row. If the count drops, you skipped the first stitch.

items.symptom: The swatch grows wider row by row
items.cause: You worked an extra dc at the end of the row — likely into the turning chain of the previous row, which on UK double crochet is not a stitch.
items.fix: The last dc of each row goes into the last actual stitch, NOT into the previous turning chain. Identify the last stitch by counting the V-shapes at the top; the previous turning chain is the small loop sticking up beyond the last V.

items.cause: The turning chain is too long, or you skipped a stitch on the first dc of the new row.
items.fix: Use a 1-chain turning chain only (not 2 or 3 chains). The first dc of the new row enters the very first stitch directly below the turning chain. The edge should sit flush.

items.symptom: The fabric curls hard along one edge
items.cause: Tension too tight; double crochet naturally curls slightly, and tight tension makes it worse.
items.fix: Block the swatch when finished — a light steam-block or wet-block relaxes the fabric flat. For long pieces, going up half a hook size (4.5 mm instead of 4 mm) often fixes the curl while keeping the stitch definition.

content.text: Once a plain dc swatch sits flat and even, the simple dishcloth in the anchor batch is a one-evening project that uses nothing but double crochet. From there, half treble (one step taller) and treble (two steps taller) are the next pattern stitches to learn — both built on the same yarn-over-pull-through structure as double crochet, just with more yarn-overs at the start.
